F-COMP: Are both fractions using the same whole? Which point lies farther right?
Draw equal-sized wholes. Mark a benchmark or rename both fractions in equal-sized parts.
F-EQUIV: How many of the new parts make one old part?
Split every original part equally. Change numerator and denominator by the same factor.
F-ADD: What size pieces must both fractions count before adding?
Draw equal wholes, rename to common-sized pieces, then combine the piece counts.
F-SUB: What size pieces must both fractions count before subtracting?
Rename both quantities using common-sized parts before removing any pieces.
F-MULT: What does the first factor count, and what does the second factor count?
Shade one factor, then take the requested fraction of that shaded amount.
F-DIV: What is the group size? Are we finding how many groups or how much per group?
Draw the total and mark one divisor-sized group. Compare the remaining part with that group.
E-EXPR: What quantity does the letter represent? How many equal groups are there?
Draw one group and label its unknown amount. Repeat the whole group before writing the expression.
E-EVAL: What number replaces the letter? Which operation happens first?
Rewrite the expression with the given value. Keep multiplication together before adding.
E-EXP: How many equal factors does the exponent name?
Write the repeated factors before multiplying. Compare that with multiplying the base by the exponent.
E-DIST: Which two quantities does the outside factor multiply?
Split the rectangle or repeated group into both parts. Count the outside factor on each part.
E-LIKE: How many groups of the same unknown are being added?
Draw one box for each x, then count the boxes. Adding boxes does not change them into squared units.
E-ADD: What operation will undo the addition while keeping both sides equal?
Draw the total as an unknown part plus a known part. Remove the same known amount from each side.
E-MULT: How many equal groups or equal fractional parts make the known total?
Use equal boxes or a tape. Find one part first, then build the whole unknown if needed.
E-STORY: Which quantities must add or multiply to the total in the story?
Label the unknown with its unit. Draw a tape that matches the story before solving.
E-RELATE: Which quantity is the input? What rule gives the output?
Label the horizontal axis with the input. Build one table row at a time before plotting.
E-INEQ: Does the boundary value satisfy the words in the problem?
Test the boundary itself. Use a filled endpoint only when equality is allowed.
G-AREA: Are we measuring the surface inside or the distance around the shape?
Cover the shape with square units for area. Trace the edge separately for perimeter.
G-PARA: Which length is perpendicular to the chosen base?
Mark the right angle. Move an end triangle to make a rectangle with the same base and height.
G-TRI: Which base-height pair makes a right angle? How is the triangle related to a parallelogram?
Pair two copies of the triangle. Find their combined area, then split it equally.
G-COMP: Which simple regions cover the shape without gaps or overlaps?
Draw one straight cut, or complete a larger rectangle and identify the part to remove.
G-SA: Which faces need covering, including the hidden faces?
Label every face on a net. Find each face area before adding the complete list.
G-VOL: How many unit cubes fit in one layer, and how many layers are there?
Draw a base layer first, then repeat it through the height. Name cubic units.
N-CONTEXT: What does zero mean here? Which direction is positive?
Name the reference point before placing the quantity on a number line.
N-ORDER: Which number lies farther right? Is that the same as being farther from zero?
Locate zero first. Count equal units left or right, keeping the unit scale fixed.
N-OPP: Which point lies equally far from zero on the other side?
Fold or reflect the number line across zero. Keep the distance and change the direction.
N-ABS: How far is the point from zero, regardless of direction?
Count unit steps from zero. A distance cannot be negative.
N-COORD: What is the horizontal position before the vertical position?
Start at the origin. Trace the horizontal move, then the vertical move.
N-REFLECT: Which coordinate stays fixed along the reflection axis?
Fold the grid along the named axis and count equal distances on opposite sides.
N-DIST: Which coordinate changes? What is the full gap between the endpoints?
Count to zero and then beyond it if the segment crosses an axis. Add the two distances.
S-QUESTION: Does this question expect different values from a group?
Compare one fixed object with several objects whose measurements may differ.
S-DISPLAY: Does every observation appear exactly once in the display?
Cross off each raw value after plotting it. Keep repeats and use nonoverlapping bins.
S-MEAN: What total is being shared, and among how many values?
Use counters to share the total equally, then connect the sharing to division.
S-MEDIAN: Have the values been ordered? Is there one middle value or a pair?
Put the values on separate cards in order. Mark the same number of values on each side.
S-RANGE: What are the smallest and largest values?
Locate both endpoints on a number line and measure their difference.
S-IQR: Are you splitting the data by count or splitting the numerical range?
Order the data and separate equal-count halves. Find the median of each half.
S-MAD: What is the mean? How far is each value from that mean?
Use nonnegative distances so the differences do not cancel. Average those distances.
S-BOX: Which markers bound the quarter of the ordered data you need?
Label minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. Compare shares of observations rather than interval lengths.
S-SPREAD: Do the sets have the same center? What evidence compares their spread?
Find the requested spread measure for both sets before making a claim.
P-SCALE: Does the same multiplier connect every pair of matching lengths?
Find the multiplier for one side and test the other sides. For area, account for both changing dimensions.
P-MAP: What real distance does one drawing unit represent?
Write the units beside the scale. Multiply or divide so the desired unit remains.
P-PROP: Is output per one input constant? What happens at an input of zero?
Compare y divided by x for two nonzero pairs, or check whether the graph passes through the origin.
P-CHANGE: Which amount is the starting whole for this percent change?
Label the starting amount for each step. Compare the change with that starting amount.
G-CIRCLE: Is the given segment a radius or a diameter? Are we finding boundary length or area?
Mark the center. Split a diameter into two radii before using the area formula.
N-ADD: Where do you start, and which direction does the operation move?
Mark the starting point. Use one unit per step and keep track of direction.
N-GCF: List the factors of each number and circle the shared ones. Choose the greatest shared factor.
N-LCM: Where do the lists of positive multiples first meet?
List several positive multiples of each number in order before choosing the first shared one.
